newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bunds recover after U.S. hit, quieten for holidays.
newsitem.headline: Bunds recover after U.S. hit, quieten for holidays.

text.p: German Bunds were dealt a stinging blow in afternoon trade on Wednesday as strong first quarter GDP data from the U.S. sent Treasuries slithering down.
Having held firm for most of the morning session, even reaching up to test resistance at 101.25, The June future was toppled by the U.S. data, sliding to a low of 100.83.
"The market took a bit of a hit on the back of the U.S. data -- as you would expect," said Norman Beauchamp, head of derivatives at Cooperative Bank in London.
DTB June futures later recovered somewhat and were quoted down 0.04 at 100.96 at 1412 GMT.

Despite domestic economic conditions well suited to a buoyant debt market, Bunds kept in step with Treasuries, unable to outperform their U.S. counterparts, keeping the 10-year cash yield spread steady at around 109 basis points.
Traders and analysts said Bunds should steady themselves for the rest of the session, settling down before Thursday's May Day holiday when German markets will be closed.
"The market has quietened down a bit now," said a trader in Frankfurt. "The big move was just after the U.S. GDP numbers."
But a slight easing in the Chicago Purchasing Managers Index did little to help Treasuries, and therefore Bunds.
The PMI slipped to 57.2 in April versus 57.5 in March but the analysts had been hoping for a more substantial decline to around 56.2.

Due to Thursday's holiday, Bunds will have to wait until Friday to react to the U.S. National Association Purchasing Management index due Thursday. Economists are forecasting a fall in the index in April to 53.6 from 55.0 in March. The April U.S. employment report is also on Friday.
On a technical view, analysts said support for the DTB June future would kick in at 100.70 initially, before a key trendline would offer further help at 100.44.
"It won't do much harm unless we take out the 100.44 level," said Beauchamp. "I think that now we're likely to stay pretty much in a range before Friday's U.S. unemployment report."
